Quebec (provincial): Regulation under Bill 16, in force 14 Aug 2025, requires every syndicat de copropriété divise to obtain a carnet d'entretien (board updates yearly, professional review every 5 years, every 10 for 8 units or fewer) and a fonds de prévoyance study every 5 years (25-year projection), first ones due by 14 Aug 2028; the syndicate must also issue an attestation sur l'état de la copropriété within 15 days of a seller's request. Preparers must be listed professionals (engineers, appraisers, architects, technologists; CPAs for the study only). Condos of 20 units or fewer are over 90% of Quebec buildings. No Quebec-specific carnet software found; French products dominate results. Candidate C1 (promising) and C4 (weak). Co-op housing boards not searched.

coverage.category: 34. Taxi, rideshare and small trucking (Ontario CVOR, federal ELD, NSC carrier profiles, Quebec PEVL and taxi permits) [overlaps category 18]
coverage.found: Ontario CVOR certificate is required for commercial vehicles (fee about $255, knowledge test for new Ontario applicants; CVOR rating from convictions, collisions and CVSA inspections). Federal ELD mandate in force since 2021, with enforcement from 1 Jan 2023; certified devices listed by Transport Canada; ELD market is mature (J.J. Keller, Geotab and others). NSC carrier profile access is limited to the carrier or its authorized agent. Quebec PEVL register: carriers need registration and a safety rating (satisfaisant, conditionnel or insatisfaisant) from the CTQ, with the SAAQ keeping the point file. CVORReady (managed service) and OxMaint (CMMS) already claim CVOR monitoring. Quebec taxi and remunerated-passenger permits not searched. Candidate C5 (weak).

coverage.category: 35. Farmers markets, food trucks and small food premises (MAPAQ permits, Ontario public-health food premises)
coverage.found: Quebec (provincial): MAPAQ restauration/vente au détail permit renews annually (2-6 week processing, fee roughly $351-540 per an older source); operator must entrust hygiene control to a certified food-establishment manager (new applicants no longer give the manager number since 8 July 2025); permit must be displayed. No separate annual declaration found. Ontario: O. Reg. 493/17 requires one certified food handler on site during operating hours (5-year certificate); special-event and farmers-market vendors apply to the local health unit, with some market exemptions. No mandatory temperature-log format found. Candidate C6 (weak).

coverage.category: 36. Export reporting and permits for small exporters (CBSA CERS, softwood lumber export charge and GAC permits) [overlaps category 30]
coverage.found: Federal: CBSA mandatory electronic export reporting since 30 June 2020 (paper B13A abolished); CERS is a free web portal, and reported declaration threshold is CAD 2,000 for non-US destinations (2020 secondary source, unconfirmed for 2026). Softwood lumber still sits on the Export Control List under EIPA, so US-bound exports need Global Affairs Canada permits (monitoring since Oct 2015; GAC allocation notices last modified Oct 2025). CRA administers the Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge; current rates and 2026 status unconfirmed. No small-exporter exemption found. No 2026 tariff-driven rule change located. Indigenous procurement and dealer 'duty to report' not searched. Candidates C7 (rejected) and C8 (unverified).

result.competitor: No product found that prepares BAO Form 2 or OPGT reconciliation. Generic cemetery software (PlotBox, Chronicle, CemSites in directories) advertises trust-fund tracking but makes no Ontario Form 2 claim. Free options already exist: OBIS online filing, BAO and OPGT guidance webinars and slides, the Trust@TheBAO.ca help line, and OPGT statements, which hold much of the data. Local accountants do the audit cases. A spreadsheet is the practical incumbent.
result.duty: FBCSA 2002 and O. Reg. 30/11 (in force, Ontario). Form 1 annual licence report is due March 31. Form 2 Report on Care and Maintenance is due within 90 days of fiscal year-end (Jan 2026 instructions). Older material said 3 months. The deadline is 180 days if an audit is required: C&M funds over $500k or a funeral establishment on the cemetery. One Form 2 per fund, filed through the OBIS portal. Enforcement: the Registrar can order an operator to stop sales under s.109(7) of O. Reg. 30/11 (example: St. David's Presbyterian, Campbellville, for missing C&M reports and trust statements). Conviction under the FBCSA carries a fine of up to $50,000 or 2 years less a day. Minimum contribution amounts were not re-checked because the PDF did not render.
result.market: Auditor General of Ontario 2020 VFM audit (Dec 2020): 2,368 cemetery operators. 1,984 reported a C&M fund. 277 (12%) were operating without a renewed licence, and 166 had not filed the C&M report for 1 to 25 years (as of June 2020). The claim's "277 operators" is wrong: that is the non-compliant subset. Most operators are small churches, municipalities and family cemeteries, many volunteer-run. No current count found.
result.reason: The duty is real, in force, and checked against BAO sources. Operators file Form 1 by March 31 each year. Form 2 is due 90 days after fiscal year-end, or 180 days if an audit is needed, with one Form 2 per fund. Missed filings lead to cease-sales orders (St. David's, Campbellville). Fines run up to $50k. I found no product that prepares Form 2. But both forms are filed once a year in the free OBIS portal. Form 2 mostly reconciles the OPGT trust statement. Buyers are largely volunteer church, township and family cemeteries with low willingness to pay. The BAO already gives free webinars and help. The claim misreads the market: 2,368 operators and 1,984 with C&M funds (AG 2020). 277 were the unrenewed operators.

result.competitor: I found no BC-specific product or police-run BC portal; the police channel is set locally and I did not verify any. Generic scrap-yard software already covers recording at purchase (ID capture, tickets, compliance rules): ScrapYardPro (US-oriented; exports police reports to LeadsOnline and BWI), ScrapRight (US-based; claims rules for all 50 US states and 'international'), BuyScrapSoftware (from US$299; captures fingerprints, ID and signatures), and RECY and ScrapWare (both in Capterra's Canadian directory). None of them showed BC Form A or Form B output in what I found. Alberta runs a separate regime that sends reports to law enforcement through a database, which suggests a multi-province angle, but I did not verify how Alberta's system works.
result.duty: B.C. Metal Dealers and Recyclers Act plus B.C. Reg. 101/2012, consolidated to Oct 6, 2026 and last amended by B.C. Reg. 61/2022. Dealers buying regulated metals must register with the Province; the Province's own registration guidance says mobile dealers do not have to register. Each purchase goes on Form A, kept on paper or electronically; if electronic, a hard copy is printed that day and kept on the premises for at least one year (s. 6). Form B goes to the local police authority before the end of the transaction day by fax, email or a police-designated website, whichever the police specify. If a technical problem stops that, the deadline is noon the next day and the dealer may also deliver in person or by courier. Printed Form B copies are kept one year (s. 7). Customer code = first 3 letters of the surname + last 3 characters of the driver's licence or BC ID (s. 4). Cash is capped at $50 for buys from the public or mobile dealers; businesses are paid by cheque. Administrative penalties and offences are set in ss. 17 and 26 of the Act; I did not retrieve the dollar amounts. The frequency is daily, for every transaction.
result.market: The BC Registrants List PDF (justice.gov.bc.ca/MetalRecyclers/Metal-Dealers-Registrations.pdf) is updated monthly, but its text could not be extracted, so I could not count entries; the copy reached carried an Oct 2024 filename. A directory site (poidata.io) estimates about 56 scrap metal dealers in BC, 66 in Alberta and 233 in Ontario. That is not a regulator count, but it points to a very small BC market of tens to low hundreds of registrants.
result.reason: The BC duty is real and current. B.C. Reg. 101/2012 is consolidated to Oct 6, 2026, last amended 2022. Dealers record each purchase on Form A, print a hard copy that day and keep it a year. They send Form B to local police by end of day, or noon the next day, by fax, email or a police website, using seller codes. Generic scrap-yard software (ScrapYardPro, ScrapRight, BuyScrapSoftware, RECY, ScrapWare) already captures ID and tickets. I found no BC-specific Form B output, so a gap exists. But the market is tiny: on the order of 50 to a few hundred BC registrants (not counted). Larger yards already run yard software, and the daily report is easy to do by fax or email. Willingness to pay for a standalone app is limited.

result.competitor: CJA/JVC plus Outlier Solutions: an interactive, on-demand AML compliance tool for jewellers, free to CJA members (valued at $2,000), plus 10% off effectiveness reviews (canadianjewellers.com/aml-with-outlier/ returned 403 on fetch; details come from the CJA aml-compliance page in search results). Substance Law sells FINTRAC compliance programs, including a DPMS page. CJA also runs FINTRAC webinars and guides. Enrolment itself will likely be a FINTRAC application form (unverified).
result.duty: Confirmed. Under the PCMLTFA, a dealer in precious metals and stones (DPMS) is covered once it buys or sells precious metals, stones or jewellery worth $10,000 or more (SOR/2002-184 s.65; this cite is from memory, and the version I found at SOR/2001-317 s.5 dates from 2008). A covered DPMS must run a compliance program with 5 elements: a compliance officer, written policies, a risk assessment, training, and an effectiveness review every 2 years. It must also identify clients, keep records, and file STR, LCTR, LVCTR and LPEPR reports. AMPs since 26 Mar 2026 reach up to $40k for minor, $4M for serious and $20M for very serious violations. Universal enrolment: S.C. 2026 c.4 (assented 26 Mar 2026) adds ss. 11.4001-11.4015, under which every s.5 entity must enrol, with periodic renewal in a period still to be prescribed. Failing to enrol becomes a criminal offence under s.74. These provisions come into force on a day fixed by Governor in Council order. That date had not been found as of Oct 2026, and the regulations were expected in spring 2026 but I could not confirm they were published. So enrolment is not yet in force and has no deadline (not_reached: the FINTRAC roadmap page returned 404).
result.market: Not reached. I found no FINTRAC count of DPMS reporting entities. Only jewellers with transactions of $10,000 or more are covered, though CJA says most retail and wholesale jewellers are DPMS. My rough estimate is low thousands of businesses, which is unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real, but the claim that no jewellery-specific tool exists is wrong. The Canadian Jewellers Association and Jewellers Vigilance Canada partnered with Outlier Solutions on an interactive AML compliance tool. CJA members get it free (valued at $2,000), plus discounted effectiveness reviews. Substance Law also sells done-for-you FINTRAC programs. Universal enrolment (PCMLTFA ss. 11.4001-11.4015, S.C. 2026 c.4) is law but not yet in force: it starts on a date the Governor in Council sets by order, and no date was found. Filing will probably be a short FINTRAC application, not much of a software job, though I did not confirm a FINTRAC portal. The market is small: several thousand jewellers at most, with no confirmed count. The trade association is the gatekeeper and is already allied with a vendor.

result.competitor: The filing itself is done in RECO's free in-house MyWeb tool. Trust accounting and reconciliation is covered by Lone Wolf BrokerWolf (back office and trust accounting, widely used in Canada), Loft47 (Canadian; escrow and trust tracking, automated accounting entries) and NexOne (transactions and disbursements), plus RECO's free Excel reconciliation template and monthly compliance checklist. I found no vendor marketing a RECO-filing-specific export, but I could not confirm that none exists. Not checked: BCFSA and Alberta equivalents.
result.duty: RECO (TRESA regulator) annual financial filing for all registered Ontario brokerages, submitted through MyWeb. First filing due 30 Oct 2026 (fiscal year 1 Aug 2025 to 31 Jul 2026); later filings within 90 days of fiscal year end. Contents: balance-sheet and income-statement line items, trust assets and liabilities, interest on trust money, unclaimed trust money, and broker-of-record attestations (including monthly reconciliations). Inactive brokerages can use a simplified filing. No CPA or LPA is needed unless imposed as enforcement. Penalties: $300 late fee, discipline referral, $2,500 fine plus $1,500 costs, suspension or revocation. Monthly trust reconciliation reporting is planned for 2027, details not yet published. A February 2026 summit proposal for an accountant to review a sample month did not make the final FAQ, which says no CPA or LPA is required.
result.market: About 3,800 registered Ontario brokerages (RECO administrator Jean Lépine, quoted by Real Estate Magazine and MPA). RECO oversees more than 110,000 registrants in total. Many are small or solo brokerages that often use outside bookkeepers.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. Every Ontario brokerage files once a year through RECO's MyWeb portal: first filing by 30 Oct 2026, then within 90 days of fiscal year end. Penalties run from a $300 fee to discipline, suspension and revocation. No accountant certification is required. The filing is a short form, about 12 balance-sheet and income figures plus trust totals and attestations, entered into RECO's free in-house tool. That leaves little for software to add. The real work is monthly trust reconciliation, which BrokerWolf, Loft47 and RECO's free Excel template already cover. The best niche is RECO-ready monthly reconciliation for small brokerages before the 2027 reporting starts. The format of that reporting is still unknown.

result.competitor: Dealer KYC: Dealertrack Canada identity verification plus an AML tool for sanctions and PEP screening; its AML page does not mention compliance programs, training or reporting, and says each dealer is responsible for its own compliance. Also AutoCorp AVA ID (an auditable identity-verification record), FraudFighter (ID checks, PEP screening, FINTRAC audits) and Patronscan ID scanners. Compliance program write-ups and reviews: MNP, Doane Grant Thornton and Substance Law (fixed-fee compliance programs, money-services focus). CFLA offers webinars and best-practice guides to members; UCDA offers FINTRAC guidance. FINTRAC's own reporting system covers report filing for free (from prior knowledge, not checked this session). I found no software built to run the whole compliance program for small lessors, factors or cheque cashers.
result.duty: PCMLTFA regulations in force: factors, cheque cashers (treated as money services businesses) and financing/leasing entities must run a compliance program, with a compliance officer, written policies, a risk assessment, a written training program and an effectiveness review at least every 2 years. They must also identify clients, collect beneficial-ownership information and keep records. They must report suspicious and large cash transactions, and discrepancies (from 1 Oct 2025). Leasing scope: business-purpose property other than real estate, passenger vehicles, and property worth $100,000 or more, so car dealers who finance or lease in-house are covered. Effective dates: 1 Apr 2025 per CFLA, UCDA and law firms; FINTRAC's "Who must report" page marks the sectors new as of 10 Jul 2025. Full compliance was expected by 1 Apr 2026. Penalties: administrative monetary penalties; one source gives $1 to $1,000 per minor sector-specific violation, with failing to file a suspicious transaction report treated as far more serious. I did not verify the final penalty schedule.
result.market: Not found. I found no count of covered financing/leasing entities, factors or cheque cashers; CFLA's linked regulatory impact assessment was not opened. Cheque cashers could be counted by filtering FINTRAC's money services business registry (open data), which I did not do. Likely buyers include independent lessors (CFLA members), merchant-cash-advance and factoring firms, and the subset of used-car dealers who finance in-house (UCDA members). The size is unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force under Canadian federal AML law (the PCMLTFA regulations). CFLA says the rules took effect on 1 April 2025 and full compliance was expected by 1 April 2026; FINTRAC's own list marks these sectors "new as of July 10, 2025". The ongoing work is recurring: KYC on every client, record keeping, reports, staff training and a program review every two years. The rush to meet the deadline has passed. Dealer KYC is already covered by Dealertrack (Equifax) and AutoCorp AVA ID; consultants (MNP, Doane Grant Thornton, Substance Law) and CFLA guides cover the program write-up. Cheque cashers fall under existing money-services rules, where vendors are already active. I found no single compliance-program software for small lessors or factors, so the gap is narrow. Market size was not found.

result.competitor: No software dedicated to the francization process (registration, assessment, programme, reports) was found in French or English searches. The Bill 96 tools I did find only cover website or storefront French: FrancoCheck and Lexibond (Shopify apps), Frenglish.ai (translation plus scanner), and app or localization agencies. The main substitute is free OQLF support: advisers who guide firms at each step, free information sessions, and an online self-assessment form. Paid help comes from consultants such as Ad Astra, working with language-law specialists, and from law firms (Miller Thomson and others).
result.duty: Charter of the French language as amended by Bill 96, in force for 25-49 employee firms since 1 June 2025. A firm with 25 or more employees over six months must register with the OQLF within six months. It then has 3 months to submit a self-assessment (OQLF form, French only), followed by a francization programme if needed, then a certificate and a report every 3 years (per Educaloi). Penalties: no public contracts or subsidies, listing on the public register of non-compliant firms, possible suspension of the certificate, and penal fines. I did not find the fine amounts in a source. Since 17 December 2025, firms with 25 or more employees must show compliance proof in LMIA and job-offer validation requests (quebec.ca). The duty mostly recurs as the 3-yearly report; the main work is a one-off.
result.market: Not verified: the claim's figure of about 20,000 firms with 25-49 employees per the OQLF. I could not open the cited napperon PDF (binary), and the quebec.ca page came back empty. OQLF annual report 2024-2025 (as summarised in search results): 3,362 registration certificates were issued in 2024-25, up 60%, and 65% of them went to firms with 25-49 employees, which is about 2,200. In total, 14,366 firms were registered with the OQLF at 31 March 2025, against 11,509 a year earlier. The 2025-26 figures were not found. The realistic number of firms is likely several thousand.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. Since 1 June 2025, a Quebec firm that has 25 to 49 employees for six months must register with the OQLF within the following six months. It then has three months to submit a self-assessment, followed by a francization programme, a certificate, and a report every three years. Since December 2025, LMIA requests also need proof of compliance. I found no software built for the francization process itself; the Bill 96 tools I found (FrancoCheck, Lexibond, Frenglish) only check website French. But the OQLF guides each firm for free, the forms are short, and the work recurs only every three years after certification. That makes it close to a one-off job with weak willingness to pay, better suited to consultants or law firms than to SaaS.

Claim correction: O. Reg. 319/08 is under the Health Protection and Promotion Act, not the Safe Drinking Water Act. It is administered by local public health units. It covers non-municipal small systems such as motels, restaurants, churches and seasonal residential systems. Duty found via secondary sources only: a Ministry of Health fact sheet says test results are kept 5 years. Owners must use licensed labs and notify the health unit. Sampling is set by site-specific directives. I could not retrieve the regulation text (e-Laws fetch returned nothing), so frequency and penalties are unconfirmed. No owner software found, but health units give free checklists and forms. No system count found; the likely scale is a few thousand scattered owners. Buyers are hard to reach, per-site directives vary by health unit, and willingness to pay is low. This is a low-value niche.
